sections.solution: Under the "Agencja Pracy Incydentalnej" (API) model, people facing multiple, overlapping difficulties can take up work as an unregistered business activity. The tasks offered are matched each time to their preferences, abilities and current life circumstances. API aims to make work as informal as possible, so that it becomes accessible to people who, at a given point in their lives, are unable to take up employment under the most common arrangements (an employment contract or civil-law contracts such as a contract of mandate or a contract for specific work). The model removes elements of employment such as the requirement to work regularly, fixed working days and hours, keeping complicated work records, etc.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the difficulty that people in deep or multidimensional crisis have in returning to the labour market.
sections.targetGroup: People experiencing homelessness and/or a mental health crisis, and/or long-term unemployed, and/or with a criminal record, and/or people with disabilities, where this crisis makes it impossible for them to take up work with set times or hours.
sections.whoCanUse: Employment agencies, organisations and NGOs working on the professional activation of people in deep crisis.
sections.doesItWork: The model shows a way to earn money legally. Taking part in the innovation enabled the target group to take up work; however, only a small part of the test group chose to use this opportunity (3 people). This is due to many barriers, the key one appearing to be a lack of readiness to make such a change in their lives, especially as it would mean partly or fully giving up social benefits. Because the project ran for a short time, difficulties arose that significantly affected the results, such as the low involvement of clients commissioning work. Given the complexity of this area of support, this seems to be an achievement and a promising start for further change.

sections.solution: The guide prepared as part of the innovation contains information on how to support children on the autism spectrum. It includes, among other things, guidance on the knowledge that people around them should be given in order to increase the chances of adjustment and integration into society. The guide aims to support both carers and teachers, who, thanks to access to up-to-date, modern ways of working with a child, will be able to provide education for children on the autism spectrum. An online observation diary, prepared at the same time, is a tool for observing important aspects of children's behaviour both at home and at nursery school. It makes it possible to spot new behaviours or changes in existing behaviour patterns more quickly.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to difficulties in making contact, continuing or maintaining interaction with another person, lack of eye contact – especially at an early stage of a child's development, the inability to develop a young person's potential, and limited access to educational institutions.
sections.targetGroup: Pre-school children on the autism spectrum.
sections.whoCanUse: Pre-school education institutions, early intervention centres, schools.
sections.doesItWork: The solution genuinely helps parents and nursery school teachers / carers to think together, and in a shared direction, about the education and development of a particular child. The online tool makes it possible to observe the child's behaviour and notice the smallest signs of change, which make it possible to analyse changes in diet or in the behaviour of, for example, other household members that affect the child's behaviour at nursery school, or the other way round.

sections.solution: Bajkala is a set made up of a wooden LED lamp with a built-in MP3 player that plays a recording of a fairy tale, an original version of the fairy tale in Polish and Russian/Chechen, a booklet with the text of the fairy tale in Polish and Russian/Chechen, and a short glossary. Besides giving soft light, the lamp plays recordings of fairy tales from Polish culture that have important similarities to stories from the listener's own culture.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the challenge of effectively integrating Chechen migrants (especially children), whose ability to function well in a new country is limited by cultural, language, legal and psychological barriers.
sections.targetGroup: Chechen children living in Poland in the care of their family, with a residence status that allows the family to live independently
sections.whoCanUse: Migrant centres, primary schools attended by migrants, and NGOs that support the active integration of refugees.
sections.doesItWork: The activities carried out showed that the mechanism was effective in motivating children to listen to Polish fairy tales and in developing their language skills. The house shape itself also proved effective in creating an atmosphere that supports development, and through positive associations it helped create a sense of safety and comfort. At the same time, long-term effects would require a much larger scale of activity and more content available within this solution. However, based on experience with the test group, the innovation seems to have the potential to support the integration of Chechen children into Polish culture and to increase their sense of comfort in the very difficult situation that refugee children are in.

sections.solution: A set of psychoeducational materials in the form of worksheets and exercises for children and young people who are struggling to return to social and school life after an absence caused by long-term therapy or psychiatric treatment. The innovation also reaches the child's family and school community, creating a support network among the people closest to the child. The psychoeducational materials help the child and the people closest to them (family, teachers, classmates) to regain mental and emotional balance. At the same time, they make teachers and peers aware of the scale of the problem and increase their involvement in helping people in a mental health crisis.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the needs of children and young people with mental health problems who are returning to school after a long absence.
sections.targetGroup: Children and young people aged 10 to 13 (years 4 to 8 of primary school) who are returning to active social life after a long absence caused by emotional difficulties, therapy or psychiatric treatment related to mood disorders, mental health crises or anxiety, as well as the parents, peers and teachers of people struggling to return to social and school life.
sections.whoCanUse: Schools and other educational institutions, psychological and educational counselling centres, crisis intervention centres, psychiatric hospitals with wards for children and young people.
sections.doesItWork: The test results showed that, thanks to the innovation, among other things, pupils' well-being improved (in the area of social functioning), and teachers' and parents' self-assessment improved (in the area of knowing the tools and ways to provide support). A drawback of the solution is that similar materials can be found in other sources. Therefore, the success of the project depends on consistent, comprehensive action from many sides (which is a challenge) and on using the full set of products.

c006.title: Bez stresu do sukcesu – child-friendly neurological therapy

sections.solution: The innovation focuses on combining methods of treatment and therapy for children and infants with nervous system disorders (physiotherapy, dog therapy, child psychologist), aiming to achieve a synergy effect from the methods introduced. As part of the innovation, a model of neurological physiotherapy for children with disabilities was created, which involves the integration and synergy of the NDT Bobath method and additional psychophysical stimuli (dog therapy and a child psychologist). Introducing additional stimuli into therapy at the start of the session is intended to regulate the level of tension and allow the proper treatment to be carried out faster and more effectively.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the lack of access to effective comprehensive therapies for children under 3 years of age which, by acting on the child's mental state, make it possible to increase the effectiveness of the main treatment.
sections.targetGroup: Children with disabilities and children at risk of permanent disability between 6 months and 3 years of age, and children with developmental difficulties who refuse to cooperate with the therapist because the rehabilitation exercises go beyond their ability to concentrate and cause them discomfort.
sections.whoCanUse: Physiotherapy facilities, parents/carers, early development support centres, day and 24-hour rehabilitation wards.
sections.doesItWork: Based on the test results, it can be assumed that the cooperation of two therapists brings the expected effects (nine out of ten children/carers confirmed their effectiveness). The positive impact of a second person taking part in the therapy process was most noticeable during manual work with the child. Most of the children did not react to touch, so the physiotherapist could work much longer and more effectively. The therapist could also focus longer on working with the child's body without spending time calming difficult emotions that disrupted the therapy.

sections.solution: A simple, cheap and practical device called BiustSPINKA, which uses a slap band and helps with putting on a bra. The device is intended for women who have various kinds of movement and physical limitations because of a disability, a health condition, an accident, an illness or having the use of only one arm. It is meant to help with putting on, fastening and taking off a bra and to make this easier.
sections.problems: The solution responds to the problem of a lack of suitable products and devices that support women with a hand dysfunction in dressing on their own.
sections.targetGroup: Women with various physical and movement limitations that make it difficult or impossible to put on a bra on their own (including wheelchair users, women with a congenital disability, women with cerebral palsy, women with a disability acquired as a result of an accident or illness, women with an arm dysfunction, women after a mastectomy, women with movement disorders as a result of a stroke or surgery, and women living with obesity).
sections.whoCanUse: Rehabilitation practices, schools, hospitals, lingerie shops, health clinics, rehabilitation wards.
sections.doesItWork: The usefulness of the product lies in its simplicity and in allowing a person with a disability to be fully independent. However, testing showed that the product is still not comfortable for everyone to use. The usefulness of the product will certainly be appreciated by people with better mobility, who can fasten a bra using one healthy hand. The doubt about usefulness concerns the specific movement needed to use the product. The slap band, which wraps around the user just below the bust, has to be hit quite hard so that it wraps around the body. It also requires precise movements to fasten the bra on the device. All this means that the product will not be equally useful for the whole target group that was originally planned.

sections.solution: A mobile device (a portable indicator of compass heading and rudder angle) connected to an app, which allows blind and partially sighted people to steer a boat on their own. The device is independent of the on-board equipment. Its function is to generate precise information (current heading, deviation from the set heading, current rudder position) and then send it to an app running on the user's smartphone, which has screen-reading software with synthetic speech. At the same time, the participant is notified of changes in heading through a series of short sounds of different frequencies, which gives information faster than synthetic speech and so shortens the reaction time to changes in heading.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the lack of equipment that allows sailors with visual impairments to navigate, and to the limited access to sailing for people with visual impairments.
sections.targetGroup: Blind people, partially sighted people.
sections.whoCanUse: People with visual impairments, organisers of voyages that include crew members with visual impairments, sailing clubs, NGOs supporting people with visual impairments.
sections.doesItWork: The solution was rated very highly by both those delivering the innovation and members of the testing group, who said directly: “I no longer feel like a ‘sack of potatoes’ that someone has to move around the deck”. Blue Sea Eye is a well-designed device which allows blind people, in favourable weather conditions, to steer a boat on their own. However, to extend the device's lifespan and improve its performance, further work is needed, including moving the circuits contained in ready-made components onto a single integrated circuit and developing power filtering and power distribution.

sections.solution: An educational material containing recommendations on diet and a healthy lifestyle for children aged 4–7, available in doctors' surgeries and used in particular during preventive check-ups of four-year-olds and six- or seven-year-olds (so-called health assessments). The text of the recommendations is aimed at parents and carers, but the illustrations attract children's attention and encourage them to talk about a healthy lifestyle.
sections.problems: The innovation addresses problems such as preventing overweight and obesity in children aged 4–7.
sections.targetGroup: Children aged 4–7 who are overweight or obese, or at risk of overweight or obesity
sections.whoCanUse: Medical facilities, preschools, NGOs.
sections.doesItWork: By improving access to reliable materials, the solution is effective in increasing parents' knowledge of the principles of healthy eating for preschool children. It is also an attractive material for the children themselves, which makes it effective in increasing children's interest in the topic as well. Tests showed that the paediatrician's support in this process is key both to starting the desired changes and to making them last.

sections.solution: A method for designing and making realistic-looking artificial legs, in the form of a cosmetic prosthesis, for people who use a wheelchair. The solution was created for people who have had both legs amputated above the knee or who were born without them. The Cloudleg prosthesis serves an aesthetic and image-related purpose – it is not a medical product. In its basic form, it is ready to be cut to the right length to suit the individual needs of the user. The prosthesis is held to the body by a holding element in the form of elastic shorts.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the discomfort caused by the absence of legs in people after amputation or with a congenital absence of limbs above the knee, who cannot or do not want to use functional/orthopaedic prostheses.
sections.targetGroup: The innovation is intended for people who have had their lower limbs amputated above the knee or were born without them, who do not use medical or functional prostheses and use a wheelchair in everyday life, and for people who have recently lost their legs and are only getting used to their new appearance.
sections.whoCanUse: Individuals after lower limb amputation, rehabilitation centres, hospitals, and organisations that support the activation of people with physical disabilities, people after amputation and people who use a wheelchair.
sections.doesItWork: The usefulness of the innovation should be rated highly. The changes observed matched the needs of the target group. The proposed idea is intended to serve an aesthetic, cosmetic purpose and, if the product is reasonably priced, it may be highly useful. A risk may relate to access to the prostheses – buying a prosthesis online may cause some distrust among potential buyers who are used to being able to try a prosthesis on carefully. c014.title: Czas na aktywność!

sections.solution: "Czas na aktywność!" is an online platform for adults with Down syndrome that enables them to lead an active and independent cultural and social life (with help from volunteers) in their own town, in line with their needs and abilities. Through a simplified interface made of images and sounds, it is designed to give information to people with intellectual disabilities in a clear and easy-to-follow way.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the problem of social inactivity among a large number of people with intellectual disabilities after they finish school. They rarely take action on their own and find it hard to use what the city offers, even though it interests them; they mainly rely on activities suggested by the facilities that look after them (ŚDS – community self-help centres, WTZ – occupational therapy workshops).
sections.targetGroup: People with intellectual disabilities aged 18–25. The innovation is aimed especially at adults with Down syndrome
sections.whoCanUse: Institutions that support and provide services for people with intellectual disabilities, including people with Down syndrome, for example: Środowiskowe Domy Samopomocy (community self-help centres), Warsztaty Terapii Zajęciowej (occupational therapy workshops), schools and NGOs.
sections.doesItWork: The solution meets the needs of the target group well and allows them to organise their free time on their own and build social relationships.

sections.solution: A standardised Cross-Border Mediation Model for use in cases of parental child abduction or the risk of parental child abduction, for couples or parents of children from different cultural backgrounds who are in conflict, mainly about where the child should live and about parental responsibility. The model combines legal, psychological and intercultural solutions with negotiation techniques in the cross-border mediation process. The model is universal and can be used before a case is taken to court, during court proceedings, and also after they have ended.

sections.targetGroup: Children who have experienced parental abduction, children at risk of parental abduction, children who are citizens of different countries and whose parents are in a parental conflict
sections.whoCanUse: Mediators, lawyers and staff of services who deal with the problem of parental child abduction in their work, schools and universities attended by children from different cultural backgrounds, family support centres, and women's rights centres.
sections.doesItWork: The innovation genuinely meets the needs of intercultural families affected by conflict and is highly effective. In addition, the solution fits well with the needs of the indirect target groups: mediators and other stakeholders who are in formal and informal contact with the people directly involved in the conflict. It should be noted that in several cases the testers decided to continue the mediation process outside the project, and also took further steps, for example starting psychological therapy for themselves or their children.

sections.solution: A mobile app that works as a kind of intuitive communication tool between refugees from Afghanistan, who are in Poland after being evacuated by the Polish Armed Forces and other Polish state institutions, and Polish society. The app/communication tool was prepared in two language versions, Dari and Polish, and with pictograms to help with some words for the part of the Afghan community who cannot read or write. The app contains practical vocabulary from several subject areas, including health, education, work and official matters.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the difficulty of communicating with Afghan refugees who came to Poland after being evacuated from Afghanistan in 2021.
sections.targetGroup: The Afghan minority living in Poland
sections.whoCanUse: The Afghan minority living in Poland; staff of Polish public institutions such as healthcare, social welfare centres, consular services, offices serving foreigners in Poland, cultural institutions and educational institutions; NGOs working for the social integration of foreigners in Poland; intercultural centres.
sections.doesItWork: The planned goals were partly achieved: the tool, which was prepared and tested, allows people who can read and write to have very basic communication, but it mostly does not work for people who cannot read or write. This is not only because of the difficulty of using suitable pictograms, but also for reasons beyond the innovator's control: people did not feel ready to use this type of tool. In its developed form, the innovation largely meets the needs of people who can read and write, but it needs key changes to allow basic communication among people who cannot read or write.

sections.solution: A fencing platform that stands out from other solutions mainly because athletes can use it on their own (attaching wheelchairs, changing athletes' positions, setting the distance between athletes), because it is light enough to transport easily, and because it has a modern, reliable system for securing wheelchairs (also during sports competitions).
sections.problems: The innovation addresses the limited access to modern wheelchair fencing equipment – the equipment currently in use is outdated, heavy, costly to operate and requires help from other people.
sections.targetGroup: Women and men who practise wheelchair fencing, both recreationally and competitively in tournaments.
sections.whoCanUse: Sports clubs and organisations that run training sessions and competitions for wheelchair users
sections.doesItWork: The prototype developed at the innovation testing stage meets most of the original assumptions of the innovation, but it has not reached a mature enough form to recommend its use in its current shape. The current technical designs, gathered in the prototype's technical specification, make it possible for almost any interested organisation (a sports club, association, foundation or group of potential users) to produce the platform, but for most users the effort involved – above all the organisational effort – outweighs the benefit of having a fencing platform for their own exclusive use. It was not possible to make the platform fully self-operated by an athlete who uses a wheelchair. The solution is promising but needs further development.

sections.solution: The innovation involves the design of a special market stall table which, thanks to its features, becomes accessible to older people and people with disabilities, making shopping at the marketplace easier or even possible. As part of the innovation, four versions of the table were created, with features such as: a suitably angled tabletop; hooks for hanging a bag, crutch or walking stick; coin trays; handrails; extra shelves under the table; extra pull-out shelves; a chair/seat.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the difficulties that people with special needs face when doing their everyday shopping.
sections.targetGroup: Older people, people with disabilities, people who walk with orthopaedic crutches or walking frames, people with balance problems, people with limited mobility in their arms, people with impaired hand and finger movement, people who use orthoses, wheelchair users
sections.whoCanUse: Organisations that own marketplaces, municipal offices (gmina), educational and cultural institutions
sections.doesItWork: The innovation meets a social need – it clearly makes buying products at the market easier. However, if shopping is viewed a little more broadly, getting to the market and moving around the marketplace should also be taken into account, as this turns out to be the main barrier for customers with mobility difficulties. Without providing beneficiaries with accessible transport to the market or instructions on how to use the tables, the solution, despite its high potential, may turn out to be of little practical use.

sections.solution: The innovation is the mobile app „Dostępny Transport Publiczny”, which is a transfer of the "Zaraz jadę" app from iOS to Android. It is designed for blind and partially sighted people and allows them to use public transport safely, comfortably and without problems. The app has features such as: showing stops on a map (with a description of the stop facilities), marking the position of public transport vehicles on the map with animated changes of location, planning a route to a chosen stop taking into account the current traffic situation, and support for the TalkBack accessibility feature.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the difficult access to public transport for people with visual impairments and the lack of access to passenger information.
sections.targetGroup: People with visual impairments, people who regularly use public transport in Warszawa.
sections.whoCanUse: Representatives of Warszawski Transport Publiczny, carers and relatives of people with visual impairments, centres supporting people with visual impairments.
sections.doesItWork: The solution was rated positively by members of the testing group, although some people were sceptical because they were used to the tools they currently use. The grant recipient reported difficulties in using data from the integrated systems of public transport operators in the app, but this did not affect the testers' experience. During testing, many recommendations were made to improve the app, including keeping information about stop facilities up to date, the grammatical correctness and abbreviated reading of messages, and making the app work on older versions of Android as well.

c022.title: Accessible application form for d/Deaf people

sections.solution: As part of the innovation, 3 templates of official documents were developed and tested. They are applications for ensuring accessibility in a specific area of public services. The solution aims to make it easier for d/Deaf people to go through official procedures in places that do not provide immediate support from a Polish Sign Language interpreter.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the problems and needs of deaf people, such as: no quick way to access interpreting services in public institutions, no formal documents that d/Deaf people can understand when they want to deal with an official matter, and, as a result, the need to fill in documents in Polish (a foreign language for d/Deaf people), for example to arrange a PJM (Polish Sign Language) interpreter for a specific official matter in public institutions.
sections.targetGroup: d/Deaf and hard of hearing people who use Polish Sign Language
sections.whoCanUse: Public administration bodies, private organisations and NGOs that support accessibility for d/Deaf people.
sections.doesItWork: According to the testers, the materials prepared in the project are highly useful and effective products. The solution makes it easier for people to request an interpreter on their own. However, it should be noted that its use may be somewhat limited to people who know certain signs or symbols. Some people will need additional explanations or definitions, which in turn reduces the effectiveness of the solution. However, the needs of Deaf people will be met only if the applications are widely available: institutions include the applications in their activities/procedures; the applications are clearly displayed on institutions' websites; and the target group is aware that such applications exist. If these conditions are met, the adapted application could serve as a kind of “fast track” to further services adapted to the needs of Deaf people (to an interpreter or interpreting).

sections.solution: A navigation system for a specialist treatment centre, for example a cancer centre, based on a network of checkpoints (no installation on the user's phone is needed). Using a dedicated app, the checkpoints point the way to one another, guiding the patient "step by step" to the chosen destination. With this system, patients and users with reduced perception caused by illness or age, or who have no one to accompany them, will be able to move around the building and find the rooms they need without difficulty.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the difficulty cancer patients have finding their way in the complex layout of medical buildings (with many corners, passageways and lifts), which can lead to confusion and problems finding the right rooms.
sections.targetGroup: The innovation is aimed at cancer patients whose perception is significantly reduced because of their illness and treatment.
sections.whoCanUse: Specialist cancer treatment centres, hospitals, clinics.
sections.doesItWork: Tests carried out in the project partly proved that the intervention is effective. It was observed that the assumptions were met: patients were guided correctly and effectively to the places chosen in the test, patients were able to use the devices on their own without prior training, and they felt that the navigation system was effective in guiding them to their destination. At the same time, the low level of "coverage" of the hospital grounds with devices, the short testing period and the patients' state of health meant that it cannot be clearly stated whether such a navigation system brings the expected changes in the target group, i.e. less need to rely on help from other people, easier quick and efficient movement between different points in the hospital, and as a result greater comfort and a stronger sense of safety for patients thanks to an easy-to-use system that supports getting around the facility.

sections.solution: The innovation is an inclusive board game that teaches how to use laughter yoga to bring people together and to help older people and people with disabilities maintain good mental health. sections.solution: Source code for a plug-in to be installed in LimeSurvey (an online survey system). This code makes it possible to record and send video answers in Polish Sign Language directly, in at least one type of question. The innovation was created (written) using available libraries and APIs (Application Programming Interfaces) and adapted to the needs of deaf and Deaf people, taking into account the capabilities of the LimeSurvey program. If a researcher has planned for users of Polish Sign Language (PJM) to take part in the study and has installed the plug-in, deaf and Deaf people can answer a question in sign language using the camera on their laptop or phone.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the fact that members of the deaf and Deaf community have had no way to express their views in survey research, and that people wishing to include people with hearing impairments in their research have had no way to run surveys for them.
sections.targetGroup: Deaf and Deaf people, and researchers who want to include users of Polish Sign Language (PJM) in their results.
sections.whoCanUse: Individual researchers, universities and academic communities, research institutes.
sections.doesItWork: Putting the innovation into practice has enabled members of the deaf and Deaf community to give their opinions in an online survey system. In turn, researchers have gained the opportunity to learn their opinions on a range of different topics. Głucha ankieta has enabled deaf and Deaf people to express themselves in their own language, not only on computers but also on mobile devices, wherever they see fit. Because the plug-in is easy and intuitive to use, no special training is needed to operate it.

sections.solution: The innovation is an app that develops the communication skills of people with intellectual disabilities. It is based on themed lessons and quizzes, in which the user chooses a response to a social situation shown on screen and then sees the result of this interaction as a particular "facial expression" of the other person in the conversation.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the communication difficulties of adults and young people with intellectual disabilities and to their problems in building closer relationships with others;
sections.targetGroup: Young people with intellectual disabilities and adults with intellectual disabilities.
sections.whoCanUse: Occupational therapy workshops (Warsztaty Terapii Zajęciowej), integration schools and special schools, and NGOs that support people with intellectual disabilities.
sections.doesItWork: The solution did not work in practice. While the app was being developed, it turned out to be impossible (within the proposed budget and with the resources the Innovator had at that time) to introduce a system for reading and processing the facial expressions of the person taking part in the interaction. It was therefore decided to try replacing this with standardised facial expressions, such as emoticons, which were meant to show users' reactions in a simple, schematic way. In this form, the tool was well received by the testing group, who were happy to use the app – and so were the therapists. However, no significant effect of the tool on improving the communication skills of the testing group was observed. In addition, the app can only be used fully independently by people who can read with understanding. Some of the testers had difficulty understanding concepts that were abstract to them, such as: app, logging in, login, etc. Some people needed individual support from a carer (especially at the stage of learning how to use the device).

c031.title: Gra o zdrowie

sections.solution: A therapeutic board game that requires the player to get involved and take on different roles from the labour market (for example, employee, employer, job candidate). It helps the player discover their potential and prepare to face real aspects of the labour market before taking real action.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the limited range of therapeutic games available for people in mental health crisis, especially games about how the labour market works. At the same time, access to therapeutic activities that help people get used to and prepare for taking up employment (sometimes again) is one of the key aspects of patients' recovery, because taking up employment often protects them from another mental health crisis.
sections.targetGroup: People experiencing a mental health crisis (in particular patients with experience of psychosis, symptoms of psychotic disorders and mood disorders) who are returning to the labour market.
sections.whoCanUse: Organisations supporting people experiencing mental health crises (for example, day wards), community self-help centres, patient clubs, and also public and private schools preparing young people to enter the labour market, Ochotnicze Hufce Pracy, and Wojewódzkie Urzędy Pracy.
sections.doesItWork: The solution was valued for its simplicity and ease of use, and because one game can be split across several sessions. People experiencing a mental health crisis are often unable to focus on the game for a long time, so being able to play only part of it is a big advantage. Playing the game also led to greater knowledge of the regulations, rules and laws that govern the labour market, a more open attitude towards situations they may face in the labour market, and better skills in coping with difficulties.

sections.solution: The social innovation is a guide in English and Ukrainian to the public health service system in Poland (primary health care) – Health Guide PL for Foreigners who are staying in Poland and have the right to services under Polish public health care. The guide is available in printed form from a PDF file, in digital form as a PDF file, and as a mobile app for Android devices. The guide gives access to organised information that Foreigners can understand, and at the same time helps them gain or increase their knowledge of the options available to patients in Poland for meeting their health care needs.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the difficult access that Foreigners (people who do not speak Polish) have to the public health care system in Poland, even though they are registered for general health insurance.
sections.targetGroup: Foreigners staying in Poland legally (on the basis of employment, education and/or refugee status) and their families, especially children.
sections.whoCanUse: Foreigners (workers, students and/or refugees and their families who are staying in Poland legally with their families and have the right to free medical care under the Polish health service system), administrative staff and personnel of the Polish public health service system
sections.doesItWork: The range of results achieved is very high. Organising information that is very scattered across the system into short summaries of knowledge about specific aspects of how health care works in Poland, and making this information available in other languages, proved to be an effective tool for increasing foreigners' knowledge of their rights and of the treatment and prevention options available to them in Poland. Importantly, this applies to both target groups (English-speaking and Ukrainian). The innovation also effectively increases the knowledge of foreigners who are parents about the children's vaccination schedule and makes it easier to choose a primary care doctor (GP). What is more, the solution also proved to bring positive changes for another group: administrative and medical staff (a reduced workload in serving foreigners and greater knowledge of the health care system), and as the solution is scaled up, this may lead to major changes in these groups.

sections.solution: Himalaje Autyzmu was created for visits to medical facilities such as clinics, outpatient clinics, blood collection points and hospitals. It is a model for working with people, mainly on the autism spectrum, who show socially unacceptable behaviour, including aggressive and self-harming behaviour. The four-step method, based on specific action scenarios, prepares the patient for a medical appointment and makes it possible to diagnose a condition and start treatment.
sections.problems: Difficulties in accessing medical services and benefits for people (including people on the autism spectrum) who show challenging behaviour (including aggressive and self-harming behaviour).
sections.targetGroup: Neurodivergent adults (mainly on the autism spectrum) who show challenging, socially unacceptable behaviour.
sections.whoCanUse: Medical facilities, hospitals, families of people who show challenging behaviour, personal assistants for people with disabilities, NGOs and organisations that employ personal assistants for people with disabilities.
sections.doesItWork: The innovation is a real and effective response to problems with access to medical services. It makes it possible to plan a visit in a way that reduces the stress of new situations for people whose non-standard behaviour prevents them from using diagnosis and treatment. It shows personal assistants for people with disabilities and carers how to prepare themselves and the patient for different types of medical appointments and procedures.

c035.title: Hop hop - mobile playground

sections.solution: The solution has two parts: a set of furniture-toys that allows children to do exercises and movement games. The solution can be used at home, but it also encourages the youngest children to exercise and play outdoors. Thanks to the texture, holes and milled grooves in the mats and the extra connectors, children can build tunnels, sensory paths, obstacle courses, rocking objects and many other games. The second part is a set of scenarios to support rehabilitation at home – a collection of games and exercises with a description of how to do them, tips for carers on motivating children, a description of the type of support and therapy, and pictures showing the exercises.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the problems of declining physical fitness and frequent psychomotor difficulties, which are a growing problem among children. These problems have genetic, social and cultural causes. Supporting healthy psychomotor development, prevention and access to daily therapy are important in the life of a preschool child and their carer.

c036.title: Innotextil

sections.solution: This innovative type of clothing and its linked app allow the user to monitor their movement constantly and discreetly, and tell them in real time when they need to correct the way they walk. The leggings have a sporty style and a universal cut, and are available in women's and men's versions.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to difficulties in accessing physiotherapy services (e.g. for older people or people on a limited budget), and therefore the limited ability of older people or, for example, people after knee injuries to maintain the effects of therapy.
sections.targetGroup: The target group of the solution is older people (by doing rehabilitation on their own at home, older people can become more independent and stay physically fit) and people with mobility impairments.
sections.whoCanUse: Clothing companies, facilities specialising in rehabilitation for older people, and medical facilities.
sections.doesItWork: „Innotextil” may be an ideal solution for anyone who wants to monitor their level of physical fitness on an ongoing basis and keep up the effects of rehabilitation regularly in everyday life. Thanks to the innovation, the user can have constant and discreet control at home over whether they are doing exercises correctly, or can correct mistakes they make while walking normally.

sections.solution: The innovation is a smart tool in the form of a pill organiser fitted with sensors that detect when a medicine is taken, a light signal system that switches on at a set time when a specific medicine should be taken, and a specially designed mobile app. With the app, the carer can set specific times for taking each medicine, and receives a notification when a dose is taken or missed. The tool will make it possible to assist and support the people being cared for remotely in looking after their health.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the challenges faced by family/informal carers, for example when caring for an elderly parent.
sections.targetGroup: Older people (who manage their own long-term medicines themselves and can use a smartphone) and their carers (who check that the people they care for take their medicines).
sections.whoCanUse: Private individuals, pharmacies, pharmaceutical companies
sections.doesItWork: In view of the carers' needs defined in the project, the device should be considered highly useful, but it comes with certain challenges. The key problem is whether the people using the device are able to set it up and then operate it (for example, when errors occur). Further work is also needed to make sure the device works without faults (any problems that arose while the prototype was being tested reduced trust in the innovation and the motivation to use it), which means that technical support for the devices will be necessary.

c038.title: Językołamacz

sections.solution: "Językołamacz" consists of an app that uses augmented reality to support the development of Polish speech in autistic children aged 3–10, as well as instructions for using the app, together with scenarios for possible sessions at home or with a therapist. The app is intended for autistic children who have fully developed hearing but whose speech centres in the brain have not developed typically, or who have other biochemical changes in the brain that make it hard to learn speech naturally.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the difficulties autistic children have with non-verbal communication, that is, understanding and using gestures and facial expressions, or making eye contact.
sections.targetGroup: Autistic children aged 3-10 who struggle with a small vocabulary, communicating with their carers, expressing their needs and communicating with their peers.
sections.whoCanUse: Parents and legal guardians of the target group, teachers and speech therapists who will use the solution in sessions with the target group, special and inclusive schools, and facilities that support therapy for autistic people.
sections.doesItWork: The app was very well received both by parents who tested it with their children at home and by teachers and therapists working with early primary school groups during developmental support sessions in educational institutions. Using a mobile device (smartphone/tablet) as the medium helped to reach this target group effectively.

sections.solution: As part of the innovation, a completely darkened and soundproofed helmet was created. It allows the user to listen to binaural recordings that imitate everyday activities, which speeds up rehabilitation and improves the quality of life of people who have recently lost their sight or will lose it in the near future. Thanks to a special sound recording technique, the helmet lets the listener hear the recorded sounds and locate them precisely in space, creating the sound illusion of being in the place where the recording was made.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the inadequate level of rehabilitation for people who are losing their sight (rehabilitation that is not safe/direct/fast/effective enough) and the lack of tools that allow blind people to live comfortably.
sections.targetGroup: People with visual impairments – both those who have recently lost their sight or are partially sighted, and those who will lose their sight in the near future.
sections.whoCanUse: People with visual impairments, organisations working on the rehabilitation of blind people.
sections.doesItWork: According to the study participants, binaural recordings are a good form of rehabilitation and therapy for people who are newly losing their sight or who lost it in the recent past. The testers felt that using this type of recording can show people who are losing their sight, or who have recently lost it, what life looks like from the perspective of a blind person. During the tests, the topic of sports recordings came up many times; such recordings could encourage people with disabilities to take up sport for recreation, rehabilitation or competition. However, moving around independently, whether with a white cane or a guide dog, was the most frequently suggested type of recording for this form of therapy. Participants most often pointed out that this is the area where they have the biggest problem and the greatest fear of leaving their "safe" home. The helmet itself was a problem because of its considerable weight and closed front panel, which makes it very uncomfortable to use at temperatures close to or above room temperature.

c040.title: QR codes to help older people

sections.solution: The innovation provides tools in the form of unique QR codes for older people, generated through a specially prepared online platform. The model consists of physical patches or stickers with codes, placed on the older person's clothing, other items of clothing or personal belongings. The QR codes are meant to be a tool to help older people who suffer from memory loss, dementia or other dementia-related illnesses. After scanning the code with a phone, a person who is ready to help can access basic information about the older person.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the difficulties older people have in getting around on their own outside the home, and to problems caused by memory disorders, chronic illnesses or dementia-related illnesses.
sections.targetGroup: Older people, including people with memory disorders or dementia-related illnesses
sections.whoCanUse: NGOs, emergency medical services, primary healthcare facilities, social welfare organisational units, and public institutions working for older people, e.g. Centra Aktywności Seniorów.
sections.doesItWork: Although the usefulness of the innovation can be rated highly, the solution needs improvement, above all in communication and ensuring safety, as well as further testing (for example, at this point it is difficult to assess how durable the materials used for the sew-on patches/stickers are). The solution needs improvement in, among other things, ensuring the safety of the person who has the stuck-on/sewn-on code and of the person scanning the code who would be ready to help. The scope of data sharing should also be reconsidered, and the people who could have access to the data should be defined.

c042.title: Comprehensive support for people after lower limb amputation

sections.solution: A model of comprehensive support for people after lower limb amputation, made up of a set of logically connected activities that help people after amputation return more quickly to everyday, independent living. The model provides holistic care for people after amputation, delivered by a psychologist, a dietitian and a physiotherapist. Under the innovation, work with the patient begins with an initial interview (physiotherapist, psychologist, dietitian). On this basis, a 12-day plan for a rehabilitation stay (two stays of 6 days each) is drawn up, listing the treatments and recommendations for each participant individually. The two stays are separated by a one-month break, which participants should spend working on their own according to the guidelines.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the lack of proper support for people directly after lower limb amputation and the lack of comprehensive rehabilitation solutions for this group.
sections.targetGroup: People after lower limb amputation
sections.whoCanUse: Institutions, businesses and legal entities caring for people after amputation, local government as part of providing care services, hospitals.
sections.doesItWork: The innovation helps to prevent social exclusion and makes it easier for people after lower limb amputation to adapt to their new reality. The model increases the patient's chance of successfully moving around with a prosthesis and, as a result, of returning quickly to everyday activities. A smooth recovery also reduces the costs borne by the state for the patient's treatment. The proposed social innovation can be replicated across the whole country and adapted to the needs of the target group of recipients and users, so this organisational model can be used for people facing a range of different challenges.

sections.solution: The work model for an ETR text consultant consists of a competence profile for an ETR consultant together with a questionnaire for assessing these competences (this tool makes it possible to select people who will take part in the training and could potentially become ETR consultants), as well as a programme of training sessions/workshops that prepare people for the role of ETR consultant.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to difficulties in the professional activation of people with intellectual disabilities and difficulties in finding and properly preparing ETR consultants
sections.targetGroup: People with intellectual disabilities and their families.
sections.whoCanUse: Organisations (e.g. schools, public offices) interested in creating information about how they work in the form of easy-to-read and easy-to-understand texts, special schools, voivodeship offices, towns and municipalities (gminas).
sections.doesItWork: The innovation can be highly effective in achieving the planned positive results among high-functioning people with intellectual disabilities who show both commitment and an appropriate level of cognitive skills. Developing detailed criteria that a person consulting ETR texts should meet is an idea that both people with intellectual disabilities and those around them (organisations commissioning ETR texts, and organisations and people using ETR texts) can benefit from. Work or cooperation as an ETR text consultant can bring an exceptional benefit in the form of professional activation of people with intellectual disabilities. On the other hand, texts that have been prepared and consulted can bring positive results in the form of a growing number of people with intellectual disabilities who read, which in turn supports their development, strengthens their self-esteem and opens up new areas. For the innovation to bring the expected results, it is necessary to take into account the individual level of skills and commitment of the person with an intellectual disability.

sections.solution: The “Korytarz wspomnień” (Memory Corridor) is intended to be a place for displaying photos, visualisations and other items connected with the residents’ memories. The innovation involves adapting a separate corridor in a care home (DPS) into a kind of memorial space, which will include, among other things, photos of the residents and their carers. The space will also be fitted with special multimedia buttons which, when pressed, will play recordings containing questions and answers about the people in the photos. As a result, at any time, older people with limited memory or dementia can recall a range of information and connect facts about their own past.
sections.problems: The innovation is a response to the limited number of tools for working with people who have dementia, including tools for group work.
sections.targetGroup: Older people, including people with memory problems and people with dementia.
sections.whoCanUse: Care homes (Domy Pomocy Społecznej)
sections.doesItWork: The innovation meets the target group’s needs related more to spending time in the care home in an interesting and varied way and listening to interesting life stories of three selected residents. However, the test did not show any effect on the memory of the care home (DPS) residents or any improvement in integration. The residents have very different levels of ability to remember – for some, the installation was hard to understand, some forgot about it completely, and for others it added variety to their daily routine. The benefits of implementing the innovation are seen more in its therapeutic nature than in its effect on the memory of the care home (DPS) residents.

c046.title: MarimBaza!

sections.solution: The working model called „Marimbaza” is based on combining music with developing important social skills. It consists of activities that involve young people who study and live in special school and education centres and in youth sociotherapy centres in preparing a music event from scratch. The workshops are accompanied by work on strengthening various skills that are especially important for this group – teamwork, self-esteem, interpersonal communication, and also manual skills through making marimbas by hand.
sections.problems: Difficulties in working with young people who experience social and educational exclusion, and a lack of modern tools that have an indirect therapeutic effect on the target group.
sections.targetGroup: Young people who study and live in special school and education centres and in youth sociotherapy centres
sections.whoCanUse: Special school and education centres, youth sociotherapy centres, community day centres, sociotherapy day centres, day support facilities.
sections.doesItWork: The innovation benefited the target group by developing several areas of skills: social and personal skills, as well as manual skills. The most important group of stakeholders – young people from the sociotherapy centre – is involved in the whole project process: they take part in its individual stages and make decisions about the directions of the project's development, and in this way they can also be a role model for other students at the centre. During the project, positive effects appeared: a break from monotony, co-creating an original event, a sense of taking part in a unique project, a boost to self-esteem, and personal development through gaining experience in co-creating an interesting artistic project

sections.solution: A self-assessment tool for the accessibility of marinas and harbours on sea waters, which supports efforts to make marinas more accessible to older people with limited mobility and to people with visual and physical disabilities. The tool consists of: a marina accessibility self-assessment scheme (a questionnaire and a set of exercises to identify the needs of people with limited mobility or disabilities and ways to respond to them), guidelines for managers on serving people with special needs, and educational and information material on different types of disability and on older people with limited mobility, in the context of their needs when using marinas.
sections.problems: The innovation is a response to the lack of adapted infrastructure at marinas and harbours on sea waters for older people and people with disabilities (the average age of sailors on the West Pomeranian sailing route is currently estimated at 55–60 years).
sections.targetGroup: Marina managers and designers, as well as older people who have difficulty moving around and people with visual and physical disabilities who have experience of sailing.
sections.whoCanUse: Marina managers and designers (sea and inland marinas)
sections.doesItWork: The innovation was assessed as effective in starting changes, but only partly effective in making them happen. Achieving the intended results, i.e. making marinas more accessible and then increasing the sports and leisure activity of people with disabilities and older people, requires a wider range of supporting activities. First, activities related to funding investment and actually adapting marinas to the needs of people with disabilities, and then activities aimed at raising the knowledge and awareness of marina managers, their customers from the target group and the wider community about the sports and leisure needs of these groups.
sections.authors: Centrum Rozwoju Społeczno-Gospodarczego Przedsiębiorstwo Społeczne sp. z o.o.

c049.title: Mixed AR and VR for motor coordination

sections.solution: An app for practising fine motor skills of the hand using modern mixed AR and VR technology. The app is designed to encourage autistic children to practise every day. Together with the app, sample scenarios for therapy sessions were also created, which can be used in everyday work with children. The app supports autistic children in practising hand motor skills every day, above all grasping and controlling the movements of the fingers and hands. Thanks to AR and VR technology, children are more willing to practise and stay engaged in the exercises for longer.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to difficulties with hand-eye coordination and coordination between the brain hemispheres in autistic children, and to the lack of tools that help strengthen fine motor skills of the hand in these children.
sections.targetGroup: Autistic people
sections.whoCanUse: Parents and carers, teachers and school representatives (above all from special schools)
sections.doesItWork: During the project, the Innovators managed to develop products that meet the minimum requirements in this area, but their quality is definitely not yet satisfactory. This applies to the app itself, the quality of the graphic elements, the extent to which VR and AR technology is used, and the content of the innovation (the level of development of the needs assessment, the target model and the content of the app). This leads to the assessment that the potential of the solution has not yet been sufficiently developed and used, and that further, extensive development work is necessary in a team of diverse specialists (therapists, IT specialists, designers and UX researchers).

sections.solution: The Mobile Job Fair (MGP) is a model of support for economically inactive women living in rural areas and small towns. It is based on cooperation between local government, local businesses and labour market institutions to provide mobile public and social services that help women living in rural areas and small towns into work, by organising mobile labour market events such as a job fair, careers advice, job placement services and meetings with employers. The mobile job fair involves organising labour market events as close as possible to where economically inactive people live, using premises belonging to local government.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the problem of helping women in rural areas into work.
sections.targetGroup: The innovation is aimed at economically inactive women living in rural areas who, because of where they live (rural areas), have difficulty accessing the labour market and see no chance of finding work.
sections.whoCanUse: Municipal governments, especially social welfare centres, county labour offices, local NGOs working in the field of the labour market, businesses and employers interested in hiring staff, employment agencies and local labour market institutions.
sections.doesItWork: The overall usefulness of the innovation can be assessed as neutral. Positive effects, such as increased motivation, improved skills and knowledge, and a change in attitude among the test participants, were observed only to a limited extent. Most of them can be described as an initial "boost" for the participants. It is important to note a very significant negative effect that occurred in the project. Despite the efforts made, very few employers took part in the fair. As a result, the participants not only had no choice of possible jobs they could take up, but also found that employers had very little interest in them. The lack of job offers, even with institutional support and participation in the project, may have strengthened their feeling that there were no job prospects in their situation.
sections.authors: Charsznica Municipality (gmina) - Gminny Ośrodek Pomocy Społecznej w Charsznicy (social welfare centre, GOPS)

sections.doesItWork: Following verification, the solution was not recommended for use on its own because the support mechanism was not successfully tested; however, the tools for assessing a family's situation developed during the project may prove useful.

c052.title: Mobile support centre for older people

sections.solution: The innovation is a form of support for older people from rural areas, far away from large cities, who find it difficult to travel to town. The method is made up of the following elements: coaching for older people, as a tool to support the older person; a mobile service – the project involves bringing the service to the client's home; a service offer (specialists, tools) developed individually for a specific community and covering several areas of support (legal, financial, health prevention – proper diet and safe physical activity). The innovation provides support from specialists: a coach, an individual action plan consultant, a lawyer, a dietitian, a physiotherapist and a finance and budget planning specialist.
sections.problems: Older people often withdraw from active life and fall into low mood and apathy. They feel lonely, rejected and unneeded. They face transport problems, social isolation and difficulties dealing with official matters.
sections.targetGroup: Older people who are not fully independent and who live in rural areas.

c053.title: Mobile teaching and sensory aid for pupils/students on the autism spectrum

sections.solution: A mobile teaching and sensory aid for pupils/students with autism spectrum disorders (hereinafter ASD), which includes the equipment needed to support learning at school, at university or at home. The aid takes the form of a folding screen containing tools (as fixed or movable elements) that help people with ASD learn, for example a visual timer showing the passing of time, quick visual and graphic messages that people with ASD need when learning: “I don't understand”, “help me”, “I need a break”, a special visual bookmark that makes reading easier, and a weighted pen. The folder is complemented by a sensory kit containing: a sensory lap blanket, a sensory band for the chair, earplugs/headphones and a sensory wristband.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to learning difficulties resulting from neurodivergence/the autism spectrum and to the problems people on the autism spectrum have in getting good marks.
sections.targetGroup: Children and young people with autism spectrum disorders, and people with a statement of special educational needs.
sections.whoCanUse: Parents and carers, teachers and therapists of people with ASD, schools and universities.
sections.doesItWork: The innovation has improved the learning process of people with ASD, which was reflected in better marks. People with ASD valued the tools provided by the teaching aid, which is adapted to their abilities and needs. The elements it contains had a measurable impact on their ability to learn.

c056.title: mPatyk

sections.solution: An educational, inclusive board game that lets players take on the roles of people with disabilities and learn about the challenges they face. By bringing together two different perspectives – that of people without disabilities and that of people with disabilities – the game helps to increase acceptance and understanding of people living with various impairments.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to a lack of understanding of the needs and difficulties of people with different types of disability.
sections.targetGroup: Children and young people – especially from settings where education on social adjustment is hard to come by – and people with disabilities.
sections.whoCanUse: Centres supporting people with disabilities, primary and secondary schools, and youth education centres.
sections.doesItWork: The game not only raises players' knowledge of the lives of people with disabilities, but also increases empathy and understanding of their problems. By encouraging players to look at the world from a different perspective, and through shared play and interaction, it is possible to promote an inclusive and understanding society that respects diversity and the needs of every individual. Simply reading the tasks – that is, possible situations that may cause difficulties for people with disabilities – has great educational value, which is further increased by coming up with the best ways to deal with each situation.

sections.solution: An app based on an indoor navigation system (iBeacon), with three separate, interactive museum tour routes adapted to the specific needs of people with visual, hearing and mobility impairments. The app starts when the visitor passes through the gate of the building and guides them along a route that suits them (for example, it only uses routes accessible to wheelchairs – so it suggests a route with a lift straight away, instead of showing how to get to the next floor by the stairs). In the profile for a person with a visual impairment, it turns on audio description, and in the profile for a deaf or Deaf person, it shows a video with Polish Sign Language (PJM) interpretation (also for exhibits where it is not possible to install a screen with PJM interpretation).
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the limited access of people with disabilities to what cultural institutions offer, and to the limited ability to visit a museum independently and explore the exhibits freely for people who need alternative ways of using the space or learning about works of art.
sections.targetGroup: People with mobility, hearing or visual impairments who, because of their disabilities, find it difficult to access what cultural institutions offer.
sections.whoCanUse: Museums, galleries and cultural venues that organise exhibitions.
sections.doesItWork: Thanks to the innovation, people with different types of disabilities (for example, mobility or visual) have gained wider access to what cultural institutions offer. In this way, their independence and self-esteem have also increased.

sections.solution: A web application for people with disabilities. It helps them plan journeys on their own and spend their time actively by giving them information about how accessible public buildings and venues are (restaurants and cafés, cultural venues, public offices, service points). After visiting places of their choice, representatives of the app's users can write a review, stating the width and slope of the ramp, whether it is possible to move around freely, and so on. This allows users to build together a real, interactive map of accessible places.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the lack of access for people with disabilities to public places, including restaurants, cafés, public offices, museums, urban infrastructure and so on, as well as to the social exclusion of people with disabilities.
sections.targetGroup: People with disabilities who have limited mobility
sections.whoCanUse: People with different types of disability, their carers/families, and centres supporting people with disabilities.
sections.doesItWork: Participants rated the app positively – its web version is much more convenient for people with disabilities who may have difficulties with fine motor skills or precise movements. All testers' comments were taken into account; among other things, automatic location of the user on the map was added, because not every user was able to type in a street name. During the testing, the accessibility of 313 places was assessed, while the app was being tested and developed at the same time.

sections.problems: The innovation responds to the need to support blind and partially sighted people in using public buildings, such as offices, museums, cultural centres, health clinics, etc., independently, easily and safely.

c061.title: Disability as an opportunity for full ability at work and in life

sections.solution: A socio-therapeutic work model for people (secondary school students) with moderate intellectual disabilities, which will increase their access to the labour market. The activities organised as part of the innovation are meant to ensure the all-round development of students and to prepare them for social roles, including roles as employees, so that they can integrate into their community as adults in the best possible way. The core of this solution is to introduce young people with disabilities to the sectors of the economy in which they can find work, to identify their strengths and weaknesses in a work context, and to determine as precisely as possible the best future workplace for them.
sections.problems: The innovation counters social exclusion, learned helplessness and a lack of influence over one's own career path. It responds to the low level of research on the open and hidden needs of people (young people) with intellectual disabilities in the context of getting into work.
sections.targetGroup: The innovation is aimed at people with moderate intellectual disabilities who need specialist help to strengthen their independence in adult life.
sections.whoCanUse: Occupational Therapy Workshops, Community Self-Help Homes, Vocational Activity Centres, and NGOs that organise support for the target group.
sections.doesItWork: Tests showed that the planned activities give young people the chance to take an active part in gaining knowledge and work experience, strengthen their social skills and will very likely help them find their place in the labour market in the near future. The young people had the chance to try themselves out in different occupations and decide how interested they were in each of them, as well as identify their strengths and weaknesses when trying new work challenges.
sections.authors: Stowarzyszenie „Razem przy Specjalnym Ośrodku Szkolno-Wychowawczym w Siedlcach”

sections.solution: The "NIEwypaleni" working model is a set of tools to prevent job burnout among people with intellectual disabilities and consists of two elements: a 3-day workshop, during which participants learn about a tool for self-directed work, that is, a booklet used during the workshop and after it ends. It was written in easy-to-read and easy-to-understand text (the ETR standard). The booklet describes activities that are worth doing to make work more enjoyable for yourself, as well as information about the symptoms of job burnout and appropriate and inappropriate behaviour in the workplace. a booklet for self-directed work, which motivates users to stay in the same workplace for a longer period of time, and to return to work if previous attempts to find and keep a job have not succeeded.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the difficulties people with intellectual disabilities have in keeping a job and to their faster job burnout.
sections.targetGroup: People with intellectual disabilities
sections.whoCanUse: Organisations offering support to people with intellectual disabilities, employers who employ people with intellectual disabilities.
sections.doesItWork: The solution developed has the potential to bring about the intended long-term changes; however, to obtain more reliable results, further testing on a larger group of people and over a longer period is required. Testing the booklet also requires the involvement of the carers of people with disabilities. To be able to assess changes in the target group, it is necessary to carry out continuous activities that remind and motivate people to develop new attitudes independently. Regular support is key to achieving the intended goals. A one-off external intervention, such as organising workshops once or handing over a publication, will not bring the intended long-term effects.

sections.solution: The innovation is a model of indoor footwear for older people. The footwear is non-slip, fits the foot well and is antibacterial, which makes it easy to keep clean. Care was also taken to make the footwear easy to put on and to keep the feet warm and comfortable. It is made of wool, which wicks away moisture well and resists odours, does not irritate the skin and, because of its properties, is recommended in the treatment of many conditions.
sections.problems: The innovation is a response to the increased risk of falls among older people – according to research, one in three people over the age of 65 is at risk of falling at least once a year. Most accidents happen at home (80% of accidents in the 85–89 age group). One of the causes is slippery floors and unsuitable, poorly chosen indoor footwear. Most older people who break a bone in a fall do not fully recover their physical abilities and often need help or support from those around them. In addition, the fear of falling alone can stop an older person from being physically active at all.
sections.targetGroup: Older people over the age of 65 with impaired fine and/or gross motor skills (including problems with the shape of the foot, e.g. bunions) and with visual impairments.
sections.whoCanUse: Businesses that make footwear, support centres for older people (municipal day care centres, care homes, etc.), sanatoriums, rehabilitation centres, private individuals.
sections.doesItWork: The indoor footwear designed in this project helps to improve the mobility and safety of older people. Thanks to the special footwear, older people move more confidently and become more independent. The footwear can be used successfully at home as well as in hospital or at a sanatorium.

sections.solution: An eco-friendly marketplace for used items in the form of a mobile app, which lets people who have items they no longer need get rid of them and, at the same time, support charitable causes. When giving away used items, the “giver” chooses a specific charitable cause, which will receive a symbolic amount paid by the “receiver”. The receiver, in turn, gets the used item by paying a small amount set by the “giver” (e.g. 5, 10 or 15 zł). At the same time, both sides support a real charitable cause chosen by the “giver”.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the lack of access to high-quality, durable everyday items for people on low incomes, the limited development of local organisations, the breakdown of local communities and the littering of the planet.
sections.targetGroup: People living in poverty
sections.whoCanUse: Local NGOs, towns and municipalities (gminas).
sections.doesItWork: The idea of an exchange platform involving 3 parties (the giver, the receiver and a charitable organisation) seems promising for the future, but in the micro version used during testing it did not deliver the full scale of results (it only indicated them). The innovators confirmed their hypotheses: first, that there is strong interest among people who have items they no longer need (in giving them away for free, thereby supporting charitable organisations and promoting eco-friendly attitudes). Second, that people are willing to choose the alternative of getting a used item instead of buying a new one, provided that this supports the ecological movement and the donation goes to the account of a charitable organisation. Third, that foundations and associations are willing to cooperate (mainly for financial reasons). However, changes in the target groups depend on the need to expand and spread the proposed solution – only a larger number of givers and receivers gives the platform a chance to work smoothly and achieve the expected benefits.

sections.solution: Oncotriada is a working method that gives female cancer patients (after diagnosis but before treatment begins) suitable support and helps set up the treatment process in the form of an oncotriad – that is, a joint meeting of a psycho-oncologist, a cancer patient in remission who acts as a volunteer, and a newly diagnosed patient.

c066.title: Home-based comprehensive care organiser

sections.solution: The home-based comprehensive care organiser is a programme of work with older people who have many health complaints, and with people whose health and ability to function have suddenly got worse. The main aim of this method is to urgently organise help in many areas for dependent people who need care at home, and for their carers, after a stay in hospital. Support is given where the dependent person lives and takes into account both the needs and the real ability of the patient's family to provide care.
sections.problems: The innovation responds to the confusion of family members or carers when a person who needs constant medical support suddenly comes home, and to the difficulties of organising care and providing the necessary equipment.
sections.targetGroup: The innovation can be used by people who are well enough to leave hospital but need intensive home care because of advanced age, which makes recovery harder, or because their health and independence changed significantly while they were in hospital. At the same time, the innovation supports people who live with the patient and become their natural carers.
sections.whoCanUse: The model can be used by organisations that manage the work of nurses (especially in long-term care), and also by local government organisational units that would like to introduce the „Organizator kompleksowej opieki w miejscu zamieszkania” (home-based comprehensive care organiser), for example as a specialist care service.
sections.doesItWork: Putting the "Organizator kompleksowej opieki w miejscu zamieszkania" (home-based comprehensive care organiser) model into practice effectively helps families facing the challenge of caring for a sick relative and removes the stress linked to this situation.
